blocks.text: A point on the graph where its derivative is zero is called a stationary point.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
At a stationary point the tangent line is horizontal (slope 0): for a moment the graph is neither rising nor falling. The name says it: the graph "stands still" there.
Our example: for \(f(x) = x^{2}\), \(f'(x) = 2x = 0\) at \(x = 0\), so \((0, 0)\) is a stationary point; it is the bottom of the parabola.
A stationary point need not be a turning point: \(g(x) = x^{3}\) has \(g'(0) = 0\), yet \(g\) increases on both sides of 0.

blocks.title: Numbering note
blocks.text: The book prints "Example 16" a second time here; the first Example 16 (\(f(x) = 2^{-x}\)) is in 2.9. We keep the printed number.

blocks.title: Example 16
blocks.problem: Find the intervals on which the function \(f(x) = |x|\), defined on \(\mathbb{R} = (-\infty, \infty)\), is increasing or decreasing.
steps:
Given: \(f(x) = |x|\) on \((-\infty, \infty)\).
To find: the intervals where \(f\) is increasing or decreasing.
Method: \(|x|\) has two formulas, one for \(x \ge 0\) and one for \(x < 0\). Differentiate each piece, check \(x = 0\) (where the formulas meet) by the definition of the derivative, then read the sign of \(f'\) on each side.

Step 1: Write \(|x|\) piece by piece
\[f(x) = |x| = \begin{cases} x & \text{if } x \ge 0 \\ -x & \text{if } x < 0 \end{cases}\]
Why: this is the definition of the modulus (Unit 1); each piece is a simple line we can differentiate.

Step 2: Differentiate each piece
\[f'(x) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } x > 0 \\ -1 & \text{if } x < 0 \end{cases}\]
Why: \(\frac{d}{dx}(x) = 1\) and \(\frac{d}{dx}(-x) = -1\). The point \(x = 0\) is left out: there the formula changes, so it needs its own check.

Step 3: Evaluate \(f'(0)\) by definition
\[f'(0) = \lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{f(0 + h) - f(0)}{h}\]
\[= \lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{f(h) - 0}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{|h|}{h}\]
Why: the derivative at a point is the limit of the difference quotient (by definition of derivative).

Step 4: One-sided limits
\[\lim_{h \to 0^{-}}\dfrac{|h|}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0^{-}}\dfrac{-h}{h} = -1\]
\[\lim_{h \to 0^{+}}\dfrac{|h|}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0^{+}}\dfrac{h}{h} = 1\]
Why: \(f(x) = |x|\) is defined differently on the left and right of \(x = 0\): for \(h < 0\), \(|h| = -h\); for \(h > 0\), \(|h| = h\).

Step 5: \(f'(0)\) is not defined
Since the left-hand and right-hand limits are different (\(-1 \ne 1\)), the limit \(\lim_{h \to 0}\frac{|h|}{h}\) does not exist. Hence \(f'(0)\) is not defined. The book adds: "(\(\therefore\) x is a critical point but not stationary)"; it means \(x = 0\) (see the Book correction below).
Why: a limit exists only when both one-sided limits agree. At \(x = 0\) the graph has a sharp corner, so there is no single tangent line.

Step 6: No stationary point
\(f'(x) = \pm 1\) wherever it exists, and \(f'(0)\) does not exist. So there is no point where the derivative is equal to zero: the function has no stationary point.
Why: a stationary point needs \(f'(x) = 0\) exactly.

Step 7: Read the signs
\[f'(x) = -1 < 0 \text{ on } (-\infty, 0)\]
\[f'(x) = 1 > 0 \text{ on } (0, \infty)\]
Why: by the test of 2.9, a negative derivative means decreasing and a positive derivative means increasing.
Check: \(f(-3) = 3 > f(-1) = 1\) (going down on the left) and \(f(1) = 1 < f(3) = 3\) (going up on the right). The V-shaped graph of \(|x|\) falls to its corner at the origin and then rises.
blocks.answer: \(f(x) = |x|\) is decreasing on \((-\infty, 0)\) and increasing on \((0, \infty)\); \(x = 0\) is a critical point (\(f'(0)\) does not exist) but not a stationary point.
book_errors: x is a critical point but not stationary

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Example 16 ends with "(\(\therefore\) x is a critical point but not stationary)". It should name the point: \(x = 0\) is a critical point but not a stationary point (\(f'(0)\) does not exist).

blocks.title: Critical Thinking
blocks.text:
Every stationary point is a critical point.
Do you think every critical point is a stationary point?

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Answer to the Critical Thinking box: no. A critical point (2.9.2) is a point where \(f'(c) = 0\) or \(f'(c)\) does not exist. A stationary point covers only the first case. In Example 16, \(x = 0\) is a critical point of \(|x|\) because \(f'(0)\) does not exist, but it is not stationary because \(f'(0)\) is not 0.
In the above example, the function has no stationary point, but it changes behavior around a point where its derivative is undefined.

Conclusion: From these examples, we conclude that a function may change its:
1. Increasing/decreasing behavior around:

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: This is why both kinds of points are collected under one name, critical points, in the next subsection: they are the only places where an increasing piece can turn into a decreasing piece (or the other way round). Between them the sign of \(f'\) cannot change.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Stationary point: \(f'(x) = 0\); the tangent is horizontal.
2. \(f(x) = |x|\) has no stationary point; \(f'(0)\) does not exist because the one-sided limits are \(-1\) and \(1\).
3. \(|x|\) is decreasing on \((-\infty, 0)\) and increasing on \((0, \infty)\).
4. A function can change from decreasing to increasing at a stationary point or at a point where \(f'\) is undefined.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Writing \(f'(0) = 0\) for \(|x|\) because the graph has its lowest point there. At a corner the derivative does not exist at all.
2. Thinking every stationary point is a turning point: \(x^{3}\) is stationary at 0 but keeps increasing.
3. Using only the two-sided limit at a point where the formula changes; compute the left and right limits separately.
